To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

maximizing and matching are both disconfirmed by the present data, but maximizing describes the findings in terms of discount rates for delayed reinforcers, and matching in terms of restructuring of the alternatives.
the matching law and the maximizing principle are both supported, but that maximizing describes choice better than matching.
maximizing and matching are not competing theories of choice but compatible descriptions of the same data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: How do animals choose between two alternatives?
the relation between matching and maximizing accounts of choice behavior.

the development of a theory of choice behavior that can be applied to a wide range of situations, and with the experimental evaluation of this theory in terms of its ability to account for a variety of choice phenomena.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
matching is the more parsimonious and powerful theory, and that maximizing is the more general and useful theory.
maximizing describes the choice data in this study functionally, but matching may be more descriptive structurally.
maximizing is not a viable account of concurrent variable-ratio, variable-interval choice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the matching law is a useful description of the data, but the maximizing principle may be a useful description of function.
matching is the best account for the data in the present experiments, but that maximizing is a useful adjunct that can be incorporated into a more complete analysis of choice.
matching describes the structure of choice, maximizing its function, and discounting the value of delayed reinforcement.
The main takeaway from our work is that
matching theory is not a good description of choice behavior in the presence of a changeover cost, even when there are no other sources of bias.
matching and maximizing can be reconciled by considering the discounting of delayed rewards.
maximizing is a more powerful and flexible theory than matching.
